# Media Feed Synchronisation Using Wireless Timing Messages

## Capturing the Media Feed

A recording device is configured to capture a media feed of a scene—such as a video or audio stream—while simultaneously receiving a series of wireless synchronisation messages. These synchronisation messages are transmitted to the device over a wireless channel and serve as common timing references shared across the system. As the device records the scene, it continuously monitors for and receives these incoming messages in parallel with its primary capture function.

## Recording Time Stamp Values

For each synchronisation message it receives, the recording device records a time stamp value that indicates the precise time at which that particular message was received. Rather than relying on the content of the messages themselves, the device notes the local time of receipt for each one. These time stamp values are then stored alongside the captured media feed, creating an associated record of timing information that accompanies the recorded content. In this way, the media feed and its corresponding series of time stamps are preserved together as a unified data set.

## Collecting Data from Multiple Devices

A separate apparatus is responsible for combining the outputs of two such recording devices. This apparatus receives, from each of the two devices, both the recorded media feed and the accompanying series of time stamp values. Because both devices are exposed to the same set of wireless synchronisation messages, each device independently produces its own set of time stamp values reflecting when it received each message. Consequently, each individual time stamp value corresponds to the moment a given wireless synchronisation message was received at that respective recording device.

## Aligning the Feeds

To synchronise the two media feeds, the apparatus aligns the sets of time stamp values obtained from the two devices. Since both sets of time stamps derive from the same underlying series of synchronisation messages, they provide a common reference framework against which the two recordings can be matched. By aligning these corresponding time stamp values, the apparatus is able to bring the two media feeds into precise temporal agreement, ensuring that the content captured by each device is accurately synchronised to a shared timeline.

# Method and Apparatus for Synchronizing Media Recordings

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to media recording systems, and more particularly to methods and apparatus for synchronizing multiple media recordings captured by independent recording devices.

## Background

In many recording scenarios, multiple devices are used to capture the same scene or event from different perspectives. For example, at a concert, sporting event, or film production, several cameras or audio recorders may operate simultaneously. A persistent challenge in such multi-device recording is achieving accurate temporal alignment of the resulting media feeds. Without precise synchronization, the individual recordings cannot be reliably combined, edited together, or presented in a coordinated manner. Traditional approaches, such as manual alignment using visual or audio cues (for example, a clapperboard), are labor-intensive and often imprecise.

## Summary of the Invention

A method and apparatus for synchronizing media recordings is disclosed. In accordance with the invention, a plurality of recording devices each capture a media feed—such as video, audio, or a combination thereof—while concurrently receiving wireless synchronization messages. Each recording device stores a set of time stamp values, wherein each time stamp value indicates the receipt time of a corresponding synchronization message, as measured by that device's internal clock.

By subsequently aligning the sets of time stamp values obtained from the multiple recording devices, the system can determine the temporal relationship between the respective media feeds. Because each device records the receipt time of the same broadcast synchronization messages, the offsets between the devices' internal clocks can be computed, and the media feeds can thereby be brought into precise alignment. This enables coordinated multi-device recording of the same scene without requiring the individual device clocks to be inherently synchronized.

## Detailed Description

In one embodiment, a transmitter broadcasts a series of wireless synchronization messages over a suitable communication channel, such as radio frequency, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, or another wireless protocol. These messages may be transmitted at regular or irregular intervals and may include an identifier, a sequence number, or other distinguishing information that allows each message to be uniquely recognized by the receiving devices.

Each recording device is equipped with a wireless receiver configured to detect the synchronization messages, a media capture component (such as a camera and/or microphone), a clock or timing reference, and a memory for storing captured media and associated time stamp data. As a device captures its media feed, it simultaneously monitors for incoming synchronization messages. Upon receiving each message, the device records a time stamp value representing the moment of receipt according to its local clock. The device thus accumulates a set of time stamp values corresponding to the sequence of received messages.

Importantly, the recording devices need not share a common synchronized clock. Each device may operate on an independent time base with an arbitrary offset and, potentially, a differing clock rate. Because all devices within range receive the same synchronization messages at effectively the same instant, the sets of time stamp values collected by the different devices provide a common reference framework.

To synchronize the recordings, a processing unit—which may reside in one of the recording devices, in a central server, or in a separate post-processing system—receives the sets of time stamp values from the multiple devices. The processing unit correlates the time stamp values, matching the entries that correspond to the same synchronization messages. From this correlation, the processing unit computes the temporal offset between the devices' clocks. In embodiments where clock drift is significant, the processing unit may further compute a scaling factor to account for differences in clock rate, thereby enabling accurate alignment over extended recording durations.

Having determined the relative timing relationships, the system aligns the corresponding media feeds so that events captured by the different devices are temporally matched. The synchronized media feeds may then be combined, edited, or presented together, for example to produce a multi-angle video, a mixed audio track, or a coordinated presentation of the recorded scene.

## Advantages

The disclosed method and apparatus provide several advantages over prior approaches. Synchronization is achieved automatically and with high precision, eliminating the need for manual alignment cues. Because the technique relies on the relative timing of commonly received wireless messages rather than absolute clock synchronization, it accommodates devices with independent and imprecise clocks. The approach is scalable to any number of recording devices within range of the synchronization transmitter and is applicable to a wide variety of media types and recording environments.

---

**A Method and What Follows**

Few phrases carry as much quiet promise as the words "a method and." They suggest that something has been figured out—a repeatable way of doing, understanding, or building—and that this way leads somewhere. A method is never an end in itself. It is always paired with an outcome, an application, a purpose. Hence the natural continuation: a method *and* a result, a method *and* a system, a method *and* an apparatus, a method *and* a meaning.

At its core, a method is a structured approach to solving a problem. It transforms uncertainty into a sequence of steps, turning what might otherwise be guesswork into something deliberate and teachable. Whether in science, engineering, art, or everyday life, a good method offers three gifts: consistency, so that results can be trusted; transferability, so that others can learn and repeat it; and improvement, so that each attempt can be measured and refined.

The word that so often follows—"and"—is where the method meets the world. In technical and legal writing, for example, the familiar formula "a method and apparatus for..." signals that an idea has both a process and a physical embodiment. In research, "a method and its results" reminds us that no technique is complete until it has been tested against reality. And in personal growth, "a method and the discipline to follow it" acknowledges that knowing *how* is only half the journey; the other half is doing.

To develop a method is to impose order on complexity. To pair it with something—an object, an experiment, a goal—is to give that order a reason to exist. The two belong together: a method without a purpose is an empty ritual, and a purpose without a method is a wish.

**System and Method for Multi-Device Video Recording Synchronization Using Wireless Messages and Timestamps**

## Abstract

A system and method for synchronizing video recordings captured by a plurality of independent recording devices. The system comprises multiple recording devices, each equipped with a wireless communication module, an internal clock, and an image capture unit. A synchronization protocol enables the devices to exchange wireless synchronization messages containing timestamp information to establish a common temporal reference frame across all participating devices. In one embodiment, a master device broadcasts periodic synchronization messages to one or more client devices, each message including a master timestamp derived from a reference clock. Upon receipt, each client device calculates a clock offset and network latency compensation value to align its internal clock with the reference clock, thereby minimizing temporal drift between devices.

Each recording device embeds synchronized timestamp metadata into its respective video stream at the frame level, enabling precise frame-by-frame alignment during subsequent processing. The system may further include a compilation module configured to receive the plurality of timestamped video recordings and automatically align, merge, or composite the recordings based on the embedded synchronization data to produce a unified multi-perspective output. The wireless synchronization messages may be transmitted over Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, or other suitable wireless protocols, and the system may dynamically recalibrate synchronization at defined intervals to maintain accuracy throughout a recording session. The disclosed system facilitates accurate temporal alignment of independently captured video content without requiring physical interconnection between recording devices.

# Abstract: Media Feed Synchronization Systems and Methods

## Abstract

Disclosed are systems and methods for synchronizing media feeds captured by two or more independently operated cameras. The disclosure presents two complementary approaches: a **recording device method** and a **server-side alignment method**, each capable of achieving temporal alignment of separately captured video and/or audio streams.

**Recording Device Method.** In one embodiment, synchronization is performed at the point of capture. Each recording device maintains a reference clock that is periodically calibrated against a shared timing source, such as a network time protocol (NTP) server, GPS timing signal, or a broadcast synchronization beacon transmitted over a local wireless network. As media is captured, each device embeds timestamp metadata into the recorded feed at the frame or sample level. Because all participating devices reference a common time base, the resulting feeds carry inherently aligned temporal markers, enabling downstream combination without further correction. This method reduces post-processing overhead and is particularly suited to coordinated multi-camera deployments where devices can communicate prior to or during capture.

**Server-Side Alignment Method.** In another embodiment, synchronization is performed after capture by a remote or centralized server. Independently recorded feeds—each of which may originate from devices lacking a shared clock—are uploaded to the server together with any available metadata (e.g., device timestamps, sample rates, and codec parameters). The server analyzes the feeds to identify correlated features, which may include audio fingerprints, transient events, motion cues, visual scene changes, or embedded markers common to multiple feeds. By computing the relative temporal offset between feeds based on these correlated features, the server determines an alignment solution and applies time shifts, resampling, or frame interpolation to produce a synchronized composite output. This method accommodates heterogeneous, uncoordinated capture sources and enables synchronization of feeds recorded by devices that did not communicate at the time of capture.

In various embodiments, the two methods may be used independently or in combination, wherein device-level timestamps provide an initial coarse alignment that is subsequently refined by server-side feature correlation. The disclosed systems and methods thereby enable robust synchronization across a wide range of capture scenarios and device capabilities.

---

# Technical Summary: Media Feed Synchronization via Wireless Timestamp Matching

## Field of Invention

The present invention relates to systems and methods for temporal alignment of independently recorded media feeds, and more particularly to synchronizing separately captured audio, video, or multimedia streams using timestamp data extracted from wireless synchronization messages.

## Background

When multiple devices independently record media of a common event, the resulting feeds typically exhibit temporal misalignment due to differences in recording start times, clock drift, and device-specific latencies. Conventional post-processing alignment methods rely on computationally intensive content analysis (e.g., waveform correlation or visual feature matching), which may be inaccurate and resource-intensive.

## Summary of the Invention

The disclosed system aligns two or more independently recorded media feeds by matching timestamp values embedded in wireless synchronization messages received by the recording devices during capture.

**Core components and method:**

1. **Wireless Sync Message Reception** — Each recording device receives a common wireless synchronization signal (e.g., broadcast, beacon, or peer-to-peer message) containing one or more reference timestamp values.

2. **Timestamp Association** — Each device associates received timestamp values with corresponding positions (frames, samples, or offsets) in its locally recorded media feed, generating timestamp-to-media-position mappings.

3. **Feed Correlation** — A processing module compares the timestamp mappings from the respective feeds to identify matching or corresponding timestamp values shared across the independently recorded streams.

4. **Temporal Alignment** — Based on the matched timestamps, the system computes a temporal offset between the feeds and aligns them to a common time reference, optionally correcting for clock drift by interpolating between multiple matched timestamp points.

## Advantages

- Enables accurate synchronization without content-based analysis
- Reduces computational overhead relative to correlation-based methods
- Supports alignment across heterogeneous devices and media types
- Accommodates clock drift correction through multiple timestamp reference points

---

# PATENT DISCLOSURE

## SYSTEM AND METHOD FOR WIRELESS SYNCHRONIZATION OF MULTIPLE MEDIA CAPTURE DEVICES USING TIMESTAMPED SYNCHRONIZATION MESSAGES

---

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to systems and methods for synchronizing media capture across multiple independent recording devices, and more particularly to a recording device that timestamps received wireless synchronization messages during scene capture, and an apparatus that aligns such timestamps from two or more devices to produce temporally synchronized media feeds.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Multi-camera and multi-microphone recording of a common scene is frequently required in cinematography, live event production, surveillance, virtual reality capture, sporting events, and volumetric video applications. When multiple independent devices capture the same scene, the resulting media streams are typically misaligned in time due to independent clock domains, variable device startup latencies, differing frame rates, and drift between free-running oscillators.

Conventional approaches to solving this problem include:

1. **Hardwired genlock/timecode distribution**, which requires physical cabling (e.g., SMPTE timecode, tri-level sync), constraining device placement and mobility and increasing deployment cost and complexity.

2. **Clapperboards or visual/audible cues**, which require manual post-processing alignment and offer coarse, error-prone synchronization.

3. **Network Time Protocol (NTP) or GPS disciplining**, which can suffer from variable network latency, limited indoor GPS availability, and insufficient precision for frame-accurate or sample-accurate alignment.

There remains a need for a wireless, cable-free system enabling precise temporal alignment of media captured by multiple independent devices, without requiring the devices to maintain a common synchronized clock at the moment of capture, and without imposing tight bounds on the accuracy of the devices' internal clocks.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention provides, in a first aspect, a **recording device** that captures a scene as a media stream while wirelessly receiving synchronization messages and, upon receipt of each synchronization message, records a **local timestamp** derived from the device's internal clock and associates that timestamp with a corresponding position within the captured media stream.

In a second aspect, the invention provides a **synchronization apparatus** that receives, from two or more such recording devices, their respective captured media streams together with the local timestamps each device recorded in response to commonly received synchronization messages, and computes a temporal alignment between the media streams by correlating timestamps associated with the same synchronization message across devices.

Because each device independently timestamps a **common** wireless synchronization event using its **own** clock, the difference between the two devices' recorded timestamps for the same event directly encodes the offset between their respective media timelines. The apparatus exploits this relationship to align the feeds without requiring the devices' clocks to be pre-synchronized.

Advantages of the invention include cable-free deployment, tolerance to independent and imprecise device clocks, frame- and sample-accurate alignment, scalability to arbitrary numbers of devices, and compatibility with heterogeneous device types (cameras, microphones, sensors).

---

## BRIEF DESCRIPTION OF THE DRAWINGS

**FIG. 1** is a system-level block diagram showing a synchronization source, a plurality of recording devices, and a synchronization apparatus.

**FIG. 2** is a block diagram of a recording device according to an embodiment.

**FIG. 3** is a timeline diagram illustrating timestamping of received synchronization messages against captured media frames.

**FIG. 4** is a block diagram of the synchronization apparatus.

**FIG. 5** is a flowchart of the timestamping method performed by a recording device.

**FIG. 6** is a flowchart of the alignment method performed by the synchronization apparatus.

**FIG. 7** illustrates clock-drift correction using two or more synchronization messages received over time.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### I. System Overview (FIG. 1)

Referring to FIG. 1, a synchronization system 100 comprises a synchronization source 110, a plurality of recording devices 120a, 120b (and optionally 120c...120n), and a synchronization apparatus 130.

The synchronization source 110 emits wireless synchronization messages 112 that propagate to, and are received by, each of the recording devices substantially concurrently. Each recording device 120 captures a scene 105 as a media stream and, upon receiving each synchronization message 112, records a local timestamp. The recording devices transmit or otherwise convey their media streams and associated timestamps to the synchronization apparatus 130, which aligns the media streams to produce a synchronized, multi-device output 140.

In various embodiments the synchronization source 110 may be:
- a dedicated beacon transmitter;
- one of the recording devices designated as master;
- a wireless access point or base station;
- a broadcast radio, Bluetooth, Bluetooth Low Energy, Wi-Fi, ultra-wideband (UWB), Zigbee, or cellular (e.g., 5G) transmitter; or
- an optical or acoustic emitter (in embodiments where "wireless" encompasses free-space optical or acoustic signaling).

### II. Recording Device (FIG. 2)

Referring to FIG. 2, a recording device 120 comprises:

- a **media capture subsystem 210** (e.g., an image sensor, camera, microphone array, or other sensor) configured to capture the scene 105 as a media stream 212 comprising a temporally ordered sequence of media units (e.g., video frames, audio samples, or sample blocks);

- a **wireless receiver 220** configured to receive the synchronization messages 112;

- an **internal clock 230** (e.g., a crystal oscillator, real-time clock, or free-running counter) that provides a monotonic local time reference;

- a **timestamping module 240** configured to, in response to receipt of a synchronization message 112 by the wireless receiver 220, capture a local timestamp T from the internal clock 230 representing the local time of receipt;

- an **association module 250** configured to associate the captured local timestamp T with a position in the media stream 212, such as a frame index, sample index, presentation time, or byte offset corresponding to the media unit being captured at or nearest to the moment the synchronization message was received;

- a **storage and/or communication subsystem 260** configured to store and/or transmit the media stream 212 together with a **synchronization record 262** comprising one or more tuples associating synchronization message identifiers with their corresponding local timestamps and media-stream positions.

In an embodiment, the timestamping module 240 records the local timestamp with sub-frame or sub-sample resolution by latching the internal clock value upon a hardware interrupt generated by the wireless receiver 220 on detection of the synchronization message, thereby minimizing software-induced jitter.

In a further embodiment, the wireless receiver 220 extracts a **message identifier**, **sequence number**, and/or **payload** from each synchronization message, permitting the synchronization apparatus to unambiguously match a synchronization event recorded by one device to the same event recorded by another device. Where the synchronization message carries a **source timestamp** or nominal transmission time, this value may additionally be stored in the synchronization record.

In another embodiment, to compensate for known or estimated propagation and receiver-processing delays, the timestamping module 240 applies a **delay correction** to the captured timestamp, or records such delay parameters for later correction by the apparatus.

### III. Timestamp-to-Media Association (FIG. 3)

Referring to FIG. 3, a media stream is depicted as a sequence of frames F0, F1, F2 ... captured at successive local times. A synchronization message SYNC#k is received at local time T. The association module 250 determines the media unit contemporaneous with T—for example, frame F_i whose exposure or capture interval contains T—and records that the synchronization event SYNC#k corresponds to frame index i (optionally with a fractional intra-frame offset δ indicating where within F_i the event occurred).

The resulting synchronization record thus embodies a mapping:

> SYNC#k → (local timestamp T, media position i + δ)

This mapping is the key datum enabling downstream alignment.

### IV. Synchronization Apparatus (FIG. 4)

Referring to FIG. 4, the synchronization apparatus 130 comprises:

- an **input interface 410** configured to receive, from a first recording device 120a, a first media stream and a first synchronization record, and from a second recording device 120b, a second media stream and a second synchronization record;

- a **matching module 420** configured to identify pairs of synchronization events—one from each device—that correspond to the **same** synchronization message (e.g., by matching message identifiers or sequence numbers);

- an **offset computation module 430** configured to compute, for each matched pair, a **temporal offset** between the two devices' media timelines based on the difference between (i) the media-stream position associated with the synchronization event in the first device and (ii) the media-stream position associated with the same synchronization event in the second device;

- an **alignment module 440** configured to apply the computed offset to temporally align the first and second media streams, for example by shifting, resampling, retiming, or re-indexing one or both media streams so that media units captured at the same real-world instant are assigned matching output presentation times; and

- an **output module 450** configured to produce a synchronized multi-device output 140, such as a combined multi-view video, a multi-track audio mix, a stitched panorama, or a common global timecode assigned to each media unit of each stream.

The apparatus 130 may be embodied as a standalone server, a cloud service, a workstation, an editing appliance, firmware within one of the recording devices, or distributed logic across multiple nodes.

### V. Method of Alignment — Basic Case

Let each recording device i possess an independent clock and media capture pipeline. For a synchronization event k received by both devices A and B:

- Device A records that event k occurred at media position P_A(k).
- Device B records that event k occurred at media position P_B(k).

Because event k corresponds to a single real-world instant common to both devices, the relative offset between the streams at that instant is:

> Δ(k) = P_A(k) − P_B(k)

The alignment module aligns the streams such that P_A(k) and P_B(k) map to a common output time. In the simplest embodiment, a single synchronization event suffices to establish a constant temporal offset between two streams of matched, stable frame/sample rates.

### VI. Method of Alignment — Drift Correction (FIG. 7)

Where the devices' clocks (and thus capture rates) drift relative to one another, two or more synchronization events k1 and k2 received at different times allow the apparatus to estimate a **linear (or higher-order) relationship** between the two timelines:

> P_A = a · P_B + b

where slope **a** captures the relative clock-rate ratio (drift) and intercept **b** captures the fixed offset. The apparatus computes a and b by fitting the matched pairs (P_A(k), P_B(k)) for k in the received event set—for example by least-squares regression when many events are available—and then resamples or retimes one stream onto the other's timeline according to the fitted model. Higher-order or piecewise models may be used to accommodate nonlinear drift, temperature-dependent oscillator variation, or dropped frames.

This drift-correcting embodiment is a principal advantage: it explicitly does **not** require the devices to share a synchronized clock; it derives and continuously refines their relative timing purely from the pattern of commonly timestamped wireless events.

2. Monitor the wireless receiver for synchronization messages.
3. Upon receipt of a synchronization message, latch a local timestamp T from the internal clock.

**ABSTRACT**

A recording device and associated method are disclosed for capturing media data in a manner that facilitates temporal alignment of independently recorded feeds. The recording device comprises a media capture component configured to generate a media stream and a communication interface configured to receive a plurality of synchronization messages transmitted over a network. The device further comprises a timing component configured to determine, for each received synchronization message, a receipt time corresponding to a local clock of the recording device. A storage component stores the captured media data in association with the determined receipt times, such that the receipt times are embedded within, appended to, or otherwise linked to respective portions of the stored media stream. In operation, a first device and a second device each independently capture respective media feeds and each independently record receipt times of the synchronization messages according to their respective local clocks. Because the synchronization messages are commonly received by both the first device and the second device, the recorded receipt times provide reference points that correlate positions in the first feed with corresponding positions in the second feed. A processing component thereafter aligns the first feed and the second feed by comparing the receipt times stored in association with each feed and applying a temporal offset derived therefrom, thereby compensating for differences between the local clocks and enabling substantially synchronized playback, combination, or further processing of the first and second feeds. In this manner, the invention enables accurate alignment of media feeds captured by distinct devices without requiring a common clock or continuous timing signal during capture.
